name: Acorn
description: Seven cells, 5,206 generations to settle. Small enough to type, large enough to fill a screen.
author: Charles Corderman

name: B-heptomino
description: The B-shaped seven. It throws off a block and keeps walking — grandparent of several puffers.
author: John H. Conway

name: Barge
description: A long diamond of six cells. The skinny cousin of the boat.
author: unknown

name: Beacon
description: Two blocks a knight-move apart. The inner corners flash on and off; the blocks never leave.
author: Simon Norton

name: Beehive
description: A six-cell hexagon. Second-commonest still life in soup, after the block.
author: unknown

name: Blinker
description: Three cells in a line that flip between horizontal and vertical every generation. Period 2, population 3.
author: John H. Conway

name: Block
description: Four cells in a square. The smallest still life, and the one everyone meets first.
author: unknown

name: Boat
description: Five cells: a block with one extra corner cell. Tiny, common, and a useful eater fragment.
author: unknown

name: Brian's Brain spark
description: Four firing cells around a cooling centre. In Brian's Brain they flash, decay, and scatter — a multi-state spark, not a Life still life.
author: Brian Silverman

name: Day & Night seed
description: A compact Day & Night seed. Self-complementary rules treat this island differently than Conway ever would.
author: Nathan Thompson

name: Diehard
description: Seven cells that live 130 generations and then leave nothing. A methuselah whose last trick is emptiness.
author: unknown

name: Eater 1
description: A seven-cell fishhook that can swallow gliders and still sit down afterwards. The original eater.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Glider
description: Five cells that walk diagonally one cell every four generations. The smallest spaceship, and the one that made Life famous.
author: Richard K. Guy

name: Gosper glider gun
description: Two queen-bee shuttles back-to-back. Every 30 generations a glider leaves, and population never looks back.
author: Bill Gosper

name: HighLife seed
description: Eight cells that are not a Conway still life. HighLife's extra birth-on-6 is enough to pull this seed apart.
author: Nathan Thompson

name: Heavyweight spaceship
description: Thirteen cells, still c/2 orthogonal. The heaviest of the three standard spaceships Conway found in 1970.
author: John H. Conway

name: Integral
description: Nine cells in an ∫-shape. A still life named for a joke about calculus, not for any calculus it performs.
author: unknown

name: Loaf
description: A seven-cell still life with a bite taken out of one corner. Stable, slightly lopsided.
author: unknown

name: Long barge
description: A barge with one extra pair of cells. Nine cells, still, and a step along the barge sequence.
author: unknown

name: Long boat
description: A boat stretched by one cell. Seven cells, still, and a step on the long-boat ladder.
author: unknown

name: Long canoe
description: A canoe stretched by one. Eight cells on a diagonal, still as a boat that forgot how to float.
author: unknown

name: Long ship
description: A ship with an extra row. Eight cells of still life, one longer than the namesake.
author: unknown

name: Lightweight spaceship
description: Nine cells, period 4, c/2 along an axis. The smallest orthogonal spaceship.
author: John H. Conway

name: Mango
description: Eight cells with a diagonal shear. Sometimes called a cigar; it does not smoke.
author: unknown

name: Middleweight spaceship
description: The middle sibling of the XWSS family: eleven cells, same period and speed as the LWSS, one row taller.
author: John H. Conway

name: Pentadecathlon
description: A row of ten, sparking at both ends on a 15-generation loop. Conway found it in the first month.
author: John H. Conway

name: Pi-heptomino
description: Seven cells in a pi shape. A short-lived methuselah and a common spark in larger machinery.
author: John H. Conway

name: Pond
description: An eight-cell ring around a 2×2 hole. Looks like a beehive that ate a block.
author: unknown

name: Pulsar
description: Forty-eight cells in four-fold symmetry, breathing on a 13×13 stage every three generations.
author: John H. Conway

name: Queen bee shuttle
description: A queen-bee spark bounces between two blocks every 30 generations. The oscillator that taught guns to exist.
author: Bill Gosper

name: R-pentomino
description: Five cells that refuse to sit down for 1,103 generations. The methuselah that started the hunt.
author: John H. Conway

name: Seeds cluster
description: Twelve cells packed into a 4×4. In Seeds every live cell dies, so this is a fuse, not a still life.
author: Brian Silverman

name: Ship
description: A six-cell still life, boat plus one. Not a spaceship — it sits there.
author: unknown

name: Ship tie
description: Two ships sharing a side. Twelve cells, one object — a still-life siamese, not a collision in progress.
author: unknown

name: Snake
description: Six cells in a 4×2 S-bend. Flat, snappy, and easy to miss in a stamp sheet.
author: unknown

name: Thunderbird
description: A T of six cells. It runs for a couple of hundred generations, then the usual junk.
author: unknown

name: Toad
description: Two offset rows of three. They rock past each other every generation — a p2 neighbour of the blinker.
author: Simon Norton

name: Tub
description: Four cells on the diagonals of a 3×3. Same population as a block, completely different shape.
author: unknown

name: Very long ship
description: A ship stretched twice. Ten cells of still life on a 5×5 diamond — the long-ship ladder's next rung.
author: unknown

name: WireWorld diode
description: A one-way conductor gap. Electrons that approach from the tail side pass; the other direction dies in the pocket.
author: Brian Silverman
